notes: West leads the ♦A against 4♠. West wins the first trick as East signals violently with the ♦J. West, apparently out of diamonds, shifts to a spade and dummy wins the trick. West is marked with the ♥A for his opening bid, but there are serious communication problems even if the hearts behave.

South should cash dummy's remaining high spade, noting East's discard, and make the highly unusual play of ducking a club trick in the hope that West was dealt both the ♣K and ♣Q (or that East will not play an honor if he has one). It is also acceptable to duck a club trick before playing a second round of trump. West can do no better than return a club and South ruffs in the closed hand to draw West's remaining trump (pitching diamonds from dummy).

South leads a heart, ducked by West, and won in dummy. Dummy's last small club is ruffed with South's last trump. West can do no better than duck again on the second round of hearts, allowing South to win the trick in dummy. South can now give West a heart trick, and West, down to just clubs, will be forced to give dummy the last 2 tricks with the ♣A and the 13th heart.

South can succeed with a partial elimination as long as East was dealt exactly 2 spades and at most 2 diamonds (including at least 1 honor). To get the timing right South should duck a diamond trick early. East wins and returns a club to South. South should continue by cashing his high spades and dummy's ♦A. South then plays a club to his hand and cashes his last club, discarding dummy's remaining small heart.

South exits in hearts and dummy's ♥K forces East to win the ♥A. On the actual layout East has only hearts and clubs remaining and he is thus forced to concede a ruff and discard. West's trump winner will be the third trick for the defense, but the contract will be safe.

Note that it would not have helped the defense if West had split his honors on the first round of diamonds. South could then win dummy's ♦A, cash the top spades, and 3 rounds of clubs. In this variation either a heart or a diamond can be discarded from the dummy on the third round of clubs.

South can now succeed by exiting in diamonds. West must duck and allow East to win the trick, but East can do no better than to cash the ♥A. A heart continuation by East will allow South to discard his last diamond loser and win dummy's ♥K while a club return will concede a ruff and discard.

notes: West leads the ♦Q against 6NT. Assuming the hearts produce 5 tricks, South has 11 top tricks. If East has the ♠K then South can win a twelfth trick by leading toward his ♠Q. Alternatively, a 3-2 diamond break could provide South with the extra trick that he needs.

Furthermore, South may be able to succeed with a squeeze if either defender (presumably West) was dealt 4 diamonds and the ♠K. South may be tempted to allow West's diamond opening lead to win in an effort to rectify the count for a possible squeeze. West can shift to a spade, however, and South won't know if he should win dummy's ♠A or not.

If the ♠A is played, it will be impossible to squeeze West (as he is sitting over both South's spades and diamonds). If instead South plays a low spade from dummy, he will go down when East was dealt the ♠K and diamonds were 3-2.

South must resist the temptation to duck the first trick. He should win West's diamond opening lead, unblock the hearts, and test the diamonds by cashing South's remaining honor. If both defenders follow, South can give up a diamond trick to establish his twelfth trick in that suit. If, instead, East discards on the second round of diamonds, South can still succeed with a 2-loser squeeze when West has the ♠K along with his known diamond length.

South can cross to the dummy in clubs and run dummy's hearts followed by South's clubs. When South leads his last club winner West is squeezed in spades and diamonds. West cannot afford to bare his ♠K and a diamond discard allows South to succeed by pitching either a small spade or a diamond from dummy. In either case South leads a diamond next and either sets up a diamond trick or endplays West (depending on what is discarded from dummy).

This is, in fact, a deceptively simple deal. After South cashes the second round of diamonds and discovers West was dealt 4 cards in that suit, East becomes an odds on favorite to hold the ♠K. South should play a spade to dummy's ♠A and lead a low spade toward the ♠Q, hoping East was dealt the ♠K.

South should then knock out the ♣K in order to establish 2 tricks in that suit. West wins and returns a club to South as East is forced to pitch a diamond. South cashes 3 rounds of spades ending in the dummy only to learn that East was dealt a spade stopper. When dummy's last club is played, East must pitch another diamond in order to keep his guards in the majors.

South knows that East's last 3 cards consist of 1 spade, 1 heart, and therefore only 1 diamond. If East's remaining diamond is an honor, South can get home by leading dummy's small diamond and winning East's honor with the ♦A. South leads the ♦2 and West is unable to prevent declarer from winning his 8th trick in diamonds.

If East's last diamond is a small card, the ♦10 must be led from dummy and passed to West. West will be endplayed into giving South a second diamond trick. It would be wrong for South to play this way at the end as East is twice as likely to have been dealt 3 diamonds to an honor (20 combinations) rather than 3 small diamonds (10 combinations). The principle of split honors allows declarer to come to the same conclusion without performing any calculations.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 7♠. The only way to play the trump suit without loss is to hope that West was dealt either ♠Q9 or ♠J9 doubleton and to reach this end position with the lead in the dummy. When dummy's heart is played the defense's "certain" trump trick evaporates in a variation of the Devil's Coup.

South will need 4 dummy entries to reach this end position; 3 to take ruffs in the closed hand and 1 to return to dummy in order to play the last heart. There is only 1 entry in the diamond suit so South must try to reach the dummy 3 times in clubs. West must have ♣J10x for the contract to have a chance.

After winning West's heart opening lead there are several possible winning sequences. South can, for example, cash the other top heart and cross to the dummy in diamonds. Dummy's remaining diamond honor is cashed on which South must discard the ♣K (if South discards a small club then West can deny declarer the dummy entries he needs by playing a high club whenever South leads a low club toward the dummy). South then ruffs a heart in the closed hand.

South's next move is to play a club towards the dummy, planning to finesse the ♣9 if West follows small. South ruffs a diamond in hand, crosses back to the dummy in clubs (finessing if West split his honors on the first round), and ruffs dummy's last diamond. The third round of clubs puts the lead back in dummy and the play of dummy's last heart leaves the defense with no answer.

notes: West leads the ♥10 against 6NT. West's heart opening lead is won in dummy and 2 rounds of diamonds reveal the 4-1 break. South plays 2 more rounds of hearts and discovers that West stops that suit as well. Both defenders follow to the ♣A, but West discards a spade on the second round of clubs.

South should cash his remaining diamond winner (cashing the last heart winner is also fine) before leading a third round of clubs. West is caught in an entry shifting squeeze on this trick. If West discards a diamond South must overtake with dummy's ♣K in order to cash dummy's newly established diamond winner. If instead West discards a heart on the third round of clubs, South's heart will be high and the club trick can be won in either hand.

Finally, if West discards a spade on the third round of clubs South must play low from the dummy. East has been forced to keep a club (or South could have won 4 club tricks) and East's remaining 2 cards will be spades. South cashes the ♠A and exits with the ♠2 to East. East is forced to lead a club to dummy's ♣K at trick 13.

There are several types of entry shifting squeezes and in many of these the presence of a trump suit is an essential feature. The entry shifting squeeze gets its name from the fact that the suit that West chooses to unguard will determine where the squeeze trick will be won. South will either allow the ♣J to hold or overtake with dummy's ♣K depending on West's choice of plays.

South can now run the hearts (having been careful to leave a trump entry to the South hand). When South leads his last heart, West will be squeezed in spades and clubs. The contract is guaranteed regardless of the distribution of the East-West cards (assuming West has the ♠K) by playing in this manner.

South crosses again in spades (it is not necessary to finesse again) and ruffs a spade in the closed hand. South then cashes 2 rounds of clubs and ruffs a club in the dummy. Dummy's last diamond is ruffed by South.
South has reached the desired end position and the lead of South's last club will hold the defense to a single trump trick.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 3NT. Assuming clubs are 3-2, South has 8 top tricks and spades is the only suit that offers any prospects for a 9th trick. West is marked with the ♠A (and most of the outstanding Queens and Jacks) for his opening bid. South's general plan should be to endplay West into leading a spade.

When East plays the ♥10 to the first trick it is apparent that West has led from a short suit. South should duck the opening lead in an attempt to begin stripping West's exit cards without allowing East to gain the lead (as a spade lead through South's ♠K would not be welcome). West continues hearts, South winning in hand.

The best chance to endplay West is to eventually give up the lead in the spade suit itself. Declarer must try to reach a 3-card ending where both the South and West hands are down to 3 spades and the lead is in the dummy. The endplay is certain to work if West was dealt all of the high spades or if East's only spade honor is the ♠10. In light of the bidding, it is not unlikely that the East-West spades will be distributed such that South can succeed.

In order to come down to a 3-card ending in which only spades remain in the South and West hands, South must first lose a diamond trick. West is likely to have the ♦Q for his opening bid and South should use avoidance technique so that only West can win a diamond trick for the defense. A diamond is led toward dummy at trick 3 and, when West follows small, South must win the trick in dummy.

South crosses to the closed hand in clubs to play another diamond toward dummy. West must play the ♦Q this time (or it will be easy to endplay him with that card) and South allows West to hold this trick. West returns a diamond to the dummy (as good as anything). South should cash his remaining heart winner and finish the clubs ending in dummy (the ♣6 and ♣5 must be unblocked).

West is caught in a 1-suit squeeze on the fourth round of clubs. If West retains a small spade, a spade is led from the dummy and East must play the ♠10 (or else South would duck to endplay West). South covers with the ♠K and West wins the ♠A. South will win his 9th trick in spades by force at the end.

If West comes down to 3 honors in spades South can duck the first round of spades completely to endplay West. If East plays the ♠10 and West has not discarded any spade honors, South's only hope is to duck. If West was dealt the ♠AQJ, he is left with no choice except to win the trick and give South his 9th trick with the ♠K.

In order to guarantee the contract, South must make the counter-intuitive play of cashing the ♦A, crashing dummy's ♦K, so that the ♦2 can be ruffed in the dummy to eliminate that suit (as before the ♥K must be preserved). Declarer continues by leading a small spade toward the South hand.

If East rises with a spade honor to win the trick he will be endplayed into providing a parking place for one of South's losers. Either a spade or a club return will build an extra winner for South in that suit (South must play the ♣2 from hand if East returns a club) while a diamond return will concede a ruff and discard.

If West wins the first round of spades instead of East he will be similarly endplayed. A diamond return gives up a ruff and discard so the best West can do is to return a spade or a club to his partner. East may return a spade to knock out dummy's ♠A entry, but South can unblock the ♣Q and return to the dummy in hearts to cash the ♣A for a spade discard.

notes: West leads the ♠3 against 7♠. If it were not for West's excellent trump lead, 13 tricks would be easy on a crossruff. After winning the first trick South should try to establish dummy's hearts by ruffing out the suit. West's discard on the second round of hearts complicates matters.

West has shown at least 5-5 in the minors with his unusual notrump overcall. South must hope that West began with 2155 distribution including the ♣K and ♣Q. South should crossruff the next several tricks, making sure to keep the ♣J and a small diamond in the closed hand.

When South ruffs a heart with his last trump, a heart trick will be established in the dummy, but West's remaining trump appears as if it will be a problem. In fact, West will be caught in a rare backwash squeeze on this trick.

If West underruffs, the rest will be easy as the dummy will be high. If, instead, West discards from either minor, South's last card in that suit will become a winner and the lead of that card will act as a trump substitute and allow declarer to win the last 2 tricks.

There are several types of backwash squeezes, all of which are characterized by a defender being squeezed in 3 suits, including the trump suit. The backwash squeeze gets its name from its unusual property that the suits that West guards are all sitting over the threat cards in the South hand. This form of backwash squeeze does not gain a trick in its own right, but instead allows declarer to compensate for a shortage of entries required to complete a suit establishment.

notes: West leads the ♥9 against 6♥. South will certainly need the club finesse, but there are still only 11 top tricks (counting 2 spade ruffs in dummy, 5 hearts, the ♦A, and 3 clubs). South will have to hope for a 4-4 diamond break or some kind of squeeze in order to come to a 12th trick.

South should assume that West has a doubleton spade as he probably would have led a singleton in his partner's suit. South needs the ♣K to be with West, but with proper technique South can almost always succeed regardless of which of the defenders was dealt club length. After winning West's trump opening lead, South should ruff a spade in the dummy and cash the ♦A for a spade discard.

South's next move should be to lead a diamond from dummy and to discard a spade from the closed hand, rectifying the count for a possible squeeze. East can do no better than return a trump to South. South should continue with a spade ruff in dummy, a diamond ruff in hand, a club finesse, and another diamond ruff (claiming if both defenders follow). If West was dealt length in both minors, he will be squeezed on the play of South's last heart.

If East was dealt length in clubs he will discard a spade on the third round of diamonds as South ruffs. South finesses in clubs and ruffs another diamond. South's last trump will squeeze East in spades and clubs.

The recommended line is essentially a double squeeze even though only 1 defender will be squeezed. The squeeze operates regardless of which defender was dealt club length. When East has 4 clubs it is necessary to play as described in order to succeed (which is what makes this line of play correct).

If West was dealt length in both minors, South can succeed not only with the recommended line, but also by playing for a squeeze without the count. South can play for this 2-loser squeeze by not discarding a spade on one of dummy's small diamonds (as was recommended). When South leads his last heart West is squeezed.

A club discard gives South an extra club trick. If instead West pitches a diamond, South discards a club from dummy and continues with a club finesse. A diamond trick is surrendered to West, but West will have to give dummy the lead and the last 2 tricks.

South finesses in hearts. It is OK to draw 1 round of trump first, but West must have the ♥K for the contract to have a chance. Dummy's remaining spade (with a high trump) to eliminate that suit. A heart is played to dummy's ♥A and a heart is ruffed high as East discards a spade. South then draws 2 rounds of trump ending in the dummy.

If both defenders follow to 2 rounds of diamonds North's heart is led and South can choose which of the defenders he wants to endplay (alternatively South can lead the ♣J or ♣9 from dummy to endplay East at once). South can either ruff dummy's last heart and duck a club to endplay East, or South can discard a club on dummy's last heart allowing West to win the trick. West will be endplayed in this variation, forced to concede a ruff and discard.

If West discards on the second round of diamonds, dummy's ♦9 wins and the last heart is played, catching East in an unusual 3-suit squeeze. If East discards a club, South will ruff and give up a club trick to East before drawing his last trump. If instead East ruffs when dummy's last heart is played, South can overruff and duck a club to endplay East. Note that dummy's third diamond is vital for this endplay to come off (as it prevents East's spade from being a safe exit card).

Finally, if East discards his last spade on the 4th round of hearts, South can ruff and draw East's last trump. With both dummy and East down to just 3 clubs, a club to the ♣9 or ♣J will endplay East.

notes: West leads the ♥K against 3♠. West wins 2 tricks in hearts as East discards a diamond on the second round. West plays a third round of hearts and East ruffs with the ♠A. South, with no minor suit losers, should underruff. This precaution gives South a chance for a trump endplay if West was dealt the 4 remaining spades.

East returns a club. Suppose South wins in hand and cashes a high spade on which East discards (otherwise the contract is safe). When West was dealt 2-2 in the minors there are several ways that South can succeed from this point. The most spectacular way is to cross to the dummy in clubs, cash 2 hearts unblocking the ♦A and ♦K, followed by a diamond winner for a club discard. South then ruffs a diamond and ducks a spade to endplay West.

If West was dealt 1 diamond and 3 clubs, South must adjust this line of play slightly by ruffing a club in his hand instead of a diamond. If West was dealt 3 diamonds and 1 club, then at trick 4 South must duck East's club return in hand to win the trick in dummy. Dummy's hearts are cashed for diamond discards and South discards his clubs on 2 of dummy's diamonds. South then ruffs a diamond in hand and endplays West in trump as before.

South has to decide early which minor suit distribution he should play West to have been dealt. West can have 7 possible singleton clubs and 56 possible diamond tripletons for a total of 392 hands with 4531 distribution. West is more likely to be 4522 as he can have 28 doubleton diamonds and 21 doubleton clubs for a total of 588 possible hands.

If West has a minor suit singleton, it is more likely to be in clubs than in diamonds so 4513 distribution is the least likely of all (there are 280 possible hands). South should thus play West for 4522 distribution which is more likely than either 4531 or 4513. South cannot combine his chances so that he can succeed on more than one distribution for West.

If instead South wins the ♣A, and crosses to the dummy, dummy's spade winner will not help South. South will still have a diamond loser and, with West sitting over the ♣Q, no squeeze is possible.

Since an extra spade winner does not help South, he should duck West's spade opening lead in both hands to rectify the count for a minor suit squeeze against West. West, who cannot afford to attack clubs from his side of the table, switches to a trump. South should continue by unblocking the ♠A and crossing to the dummy in hearts in order to ruff a spade in the closed hand. South crosses again in hearts and dummy's last spade is ruffed.

South must continue by cashing the ♦A (a Vienna Coup) before running the rest of dummy's hearts (South had to be careful to unblock his hearts in order to win the next trick in the dummy). When dummy's last trump is played, West must keep his ♦K so will be forced to come down to a singleton club. South should read the position and drop the ♣K since West is very likely to have both minor suit Kings given his unusual notrump overcall.

South should duck the first 2 rounds of hearts. When East continues hearts (nothing is better), South wins the ♥A and should discard a spade from the dummy.

This unusual play allows South the luxury of guarding against a singleton ♣K with East. South should continue by unblocking dummy's spades and then cashing the ♣A. Assuming the ♣K does not fall South plays a second round of clubs which West must win to block the suit.

If West returns a diamond in an attempt to remove South's hand entry while the clubs are still blocked South can counter by discarding dummy's blocking club on his spade winner. South is now free to run the clubs and will end up making his contract with an overtrick.

notes: West leads the ♥J against 3NT. East overtakes West's heart opening lead and South ducks. When East continues hearts South should win the ♥A. A single hold up will exhaust the West hand of hearts and South will need a small heart in the event that East was dealt 4 cards in clubs.

South should test the clubs by cashing 2 rounds (9 tricks will be easy if both opponents follow). If East discards on the second round, marking West with a club stopper, South will have to guess which defender was dealt the ♦K and eventually either endplay West by exiting in clubs or endplay East by exiting in hearts. When West unexpectedly discards on the second round of clubs, East has the defensive club guard and South must change his plan.

Given that East was dealt 6 hearts and 4 clubs, West is a big favorite to hold the ♦K. In this case South's best chance for a 9th trick is to play to squeeze East in hearts and clubs. South has 4 losers and must rectify the count down to 1 loser in order for a squeeze against East to mature. South must plan on ducking 3 tricks in diamonds and hope that East is unable to gain the lead in that suit (as he could then run enough heart tricks to defeat the contract).

East's most likely distribution is 2614 (even more so given West's early diamond discard, likely from 5) and South can succeed as long as East's singleton diamond is not the ♦K. South should lead the ♦Q and duck in dummy when West covers. West shifts to a spade which South must win in his hand. Next South should duck a second diamond trick (hopefully to West). West continues spades and again South must win in his hand. A third diamond trick should be ducked to West.
West must lead a spade or a diamond, giving dummy the lead and the play of dummy's remaining winner will squeeze East in hearts and clubs.

Dummy's remaining diamond honor is cashed (South cannot afford to overtake) and South must find a way back to his hand to draw the rest of East's trump.

Dummy's top spades should be cashed for club discards. If East ruffs the second spade then South can overruff and draw the rest of East's trump. West (who is counted out to 7204 distribution) will be squeezed when South's last diamond is played.

If East follows to the second round of spades, South must hope that East's distribution is 2551 (South has no chance if East is 3550). South must cross to his hand in clubs, blocking the suit, and draw East's trump.

South's last diamond catches West in a jettison squeeze. A spade discard will set up a spade winner in the dummy. If instead West discards a club, then the ♣A is jettisoned from the dummy and South's clubs will win the last 2 tricks. Note that the jettison squeeze only gains a trick in the sense of allowing declarer to get back an unavailable trick in a blocked suit.

notes: West leads the ♦5 against 4♠ doubled. West's double marks him with all 4 outstanding trumps. As South must lose tricks to the ♥A and ♣A he will have to find a way to hold his trump losers to 1. The only hope is some kind of trump endplay against West.

South must reach this position. On the lead of South's heart West has no winning play. If he ruffs with the ♠K, West will be endplayed into giving up his second natural trump trick. If instead West ruffs with a middle spade, dummy overruffs with the ♠Q. South ducks a spade to West (or ruffs a club low) and once again West is endplayed in trump. Finally, if West ruffs with the ♠4, dummy overruffs. Dummy's club is ruffed with the ♠A and a spade is led toward dummy's ♠Q.

Assuming West has 4 spades, he must have 3 diamonds for the contract to have a chance. The only possible distribution that East can have is 0445 (some players open 1♦ instead of 1♣ with this pattern to avoid rebid problems). The timing must be precise. First, South must win the opening lead in dummy. A heart must be led at trick 2. Assume East ducks (best). South must surrender a club trick next (leading either the ♣K or a low club is fine).

The defense can do no better than return a club for South to ruff. South must now surrender a heart trick to East's ♥A. East returns a low club (nothing is better) and South ruffs (pitching the ♦3 will also lead to success). South continues with a heart ruff in dummy followed by 2 rounds of diamonds ending in the closed hand. The desired end position has been reached and the lead of South's last heart will hold West to only 1 trump trick.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 6♦. South should make the unusual play of ducking the first trick in dummy. There are 2 reasons for this play. First, at some point it will be necessary to lose a heart trick in order to establish a second trick in that suit.

Second, if a second heart trick cannot be set up, then South may require a squeeze. Ducking the first round of hearts is the only safe way to rectify the count down to 1 loser. If the defense continues hearts South should win the ♥A in dummy, discarding a spade from the closed hand.

South should then draw 2 rounds of trump, ending with dummy's ♦K. If both defenders follow to the second round of diamonds a heart can be ruffed safely and the rest of the trump can be drawn. When diamonds are 3-3 and hearts are 4-3 South will be able to ruff another heart to set up his 12th trick in that suit (the ♠A and ♣Q are the 2 dummy entries that South will require).

When East discards on the second round of diamonds, South must hope that either clubs are 3-3 or that a squeeze can be executed. South should cross to his hand and draw West's remaining trump. On the actual layout East was dealt the only defensive guards in both clubs and spades and he will be squeezed on the last round of trump.

notes: West leads the ♣10 against 7♠. West's club opening lead is covered by both the dummy and East and ruffed by South. South draws 2 rounds of trump noting that East was dealt both of the outstanding spades.

The contract is very poor. Even if West was dealt the ♥K there are only 11 top tricks (7 spades, 2 hearts, and 2 diamonds). South will need to execute a repeating squeeze in order to come to the 2 extra tricks that are needed. For this to be possible West must have the only defensive guards in hearts and diamonds as well as the ♣9 that his opening lead suggests.

Even on this layout South cannot succeed against best defense. When South leads the ♥Q or ♥J for a finesse West will refuse to cover. South will run the spades, but West will abandon his club guard on the second last round. South can now cross to the dummy and lead dummy's remaining club honor through East to pin West's ♣9. The ♣8 in the dummy has become a winner, but the entry position is all wrong for the squeeze against West to repeat.

It is, in fact, impossible to make the contract against best defense if West was dealt the ♥K. South's only hope is that East was dealt a singleton ♥K. Declarer can get up to 12 tricks by dropping the ♥K, but a squeeze will still be required for a 13th trick. Assuming East has the singleton ♥K, 2 spades, and the 7 clubs he showed with his 3♣ opening, he must be 2137. Since both defenders guard diamonds a simple squeeze will not be possible.

South's only chance is to play for an unusual type of squeeze. He should play a heart to the ♥A, hoping that East drops the ♥K, and run all of the major suit winners except for 1 spade. Both defenders will be squeezed on the second last spade (the above position is called a double trump squeeze). Dummy's ♦5 will be discarded on this trick regardless of what West plays.

If West discards a club South will cross in diamonds and lead the ♣Q through East's ♣A to pin West's ♣9. Dummy's ♣8 will be high and diamonds can be used as an entry to that winner. If instead West pitches a diamond on the second last trump, East will be squeezed in the minors. A diamond discard allows South to unblock the diamonds and return to the closed hand with a club ruff to enjoy a third trick in diamonds.

If instead East discards a club, South can cross to the dummy in diamonds and lead the ♣8 to ruff out East's ♣A. The last 2 tricks with be won with dummy's remaining diamond honor and the recently established ♣Q.

notes: West leads the ♣8 against 5♥. West's club lead is an obvious singleton which leaves South with 2 club losers. South has a certain diamond loser as well and must hope that East is the only defender with a diamond guard. In this case South may be able to arrange to squeeze East in the minors.

South should start by winning the ♣A in his hand as dummy's ♣K will be needed as a dummy entry in order for a squeeze against East to be possible. South has 3 losers - too many for a squeeze against East to be viable. South must try to lose at least 1 trick, but he cannot afford to lose the lead to East as a club return would destroy South's squeeze chances.

Part of South's plan should be to eliminate East's spades so that a 2-loser squeeze against East will be possible. At the same time South should hope to reduce his loser count by discarding a minor suit loser on one of dummy's spades at a time when only West can win the trick.

West is marked with 7 spades from the bidding and 1 club given the opening lead. West must have 2 diamonds for there to be a chance. South should therefore assume that West has 3 hearts. The dummy will have to be entered 3 times in hearts and this will only be possible when East's singleton heart is the ♥8 or ♥7.

South should lead a middle heart and overtake with dummy's ♥K, hoping to see East follow with the ♥8 or ♥7. A spade is played from dummy and, unless East plays the ♠2, South ruffs high. South crosses to the dummy with a trump finesse and another spade is led and ruffed high when East follows with a spade higher than the ♠2.

South returns to the dummy in hearts to play dummy's last spade on which East finally produces the ♠2 (the contract cannot be made if West was dealt this card). South can discard from either minor (a diamond discard makes things a little more interesting) and West wins the trick.

If West returns a diamond South can win and lead his last trump, discarding a club from the dummy. East is caught in a criss-cross squeeze without the count (a 2-loser squeeze). A diamond discard will establish dummy's third diamond as a winner, while a club discard will allow South to play 2 rounds of that suit to set up a club winner in the South hand.

If West exits in spades instead of diamonds, a club is discarded from the dummy and East is squeezed as before. If East discards a club, South can either ruff and play on clubs or discard a club himself. Another club is pitched from dummy on the next spade (or on the last heart if West now plays a diamond instead of a spade) and East is caught in a more common 1-loser criss-cross squeeze on this trick.

Some sort of minor suit squeeze looks to be the only chance, but South cannot afford to rectify the count down to 1 or 2 losers.

If, for example, West's spade opening lead is won with dummy's ♠A, trumps are drawn, and a heart trick is surrendered in an attempt to rectify the count, the denfense will always prevail, almost regardless of the layout of the East-West cards. South will then be able to succeed by running his spades (pitching 1 heart and 3 clubs from the dummy). East will be caught in an unusual 3-suit squeeze that will leave him unable to prevent South from winning a 10th trick.

notes: West leads the ♣Q against 6NT. South must win West's club opening lead and immediately run diamonds (the contract cannot be made if South cashes his other high club first). West's discard on the first round of diamonds (and his opening lead) suggest that West may well be the defender with a club stopper.

When dummy's last diamond is played, East's club discard further suggests that West is guarding that suit. South must discard the ♥K (coming down to 3 spades and 2 clubs) and, on the actual layout, West is squeezed in 3 suits. A club or a spade discard will give up a trick at once (if West discards a spade South can lead the ♠K to drop West's ♠J and then finesse against East's ♠Q) so West must come down to a singleton heart.

South must hope that East was dealt either the ♥3 or the ♥2. If this is the case South can concede a heart trick to the defense and not have to worry about losing 2 heart tricks at once (even if West has unblocked the ♥A to come down to a small singleton heart). West must win this trick (or North will later win a heart trick) as South discards his club loser.

West cannot afford to exit in spades without giving up a trick in that suit, but a club return is no better for the defense. East will be squeezed in the majors on this trick as South wins the ♣K. It is unusual that this deal ended up with East shouldering the responsibility of preventing dummy from winning a trick in hearts.

South's only other real chance is to hope that East was dealt the defensive club guard along with the ♠Q and ♠J. In this case East will be caught in a squeeze without the count when dummy's last diamond is played. East must discard his remaining heart as South discards a spade. South can now play a club to his hand and safely surrender a club trick to East to build a 12th trick.

South should discard his hearts early and keep 3 clubs at the time dummy's last diamond is played in order to preserve his chances for both possible squeezes. East's club discard (which is forced) suggests that South should also discard a club and play for the 3-suit squeeze against West.

notes: West leads the ♦K against 6♠. East wins the first trick with the ♦A. East, obviously out of diamonds, switches to a trump which South wins in hand as West discards. There is only 1 play sequence that guarantees the contract in this beautiful deal from Michael Rosenberg's book, Bridge, Zia, and Me.

Since West is known to have 7 diamonds he can have 6 hearts at most. East must therefore have at least 1 heart and it is safe for South to cash a trick in that suit. Now, since West is known to have 7 diamonds and 1 heart he can have 5 clubs at the most. East must have at least 1 club and it is safe to cash a club trick.

At this point South knows that West was dealt 7 diamonds and 1 club so he can have no more than 5 hearts. East must have another heart so it safe for South to cash his other heart winner. Similarly, once West has followed to 2 hearts he can have 4 clubs at the most. East must have another club so South can safely cash another round. When both defenders follow to all of these tricks South can ruff a club with dummy's ♠K and draw trump.

If West had discarded on the second round of clubs (marking him with 0571 distribution) there would be several winning lines. South could, for example, cash his remaining high club, ruff a club low, and crossruff high.

If West had shown out on the first or second round of hearts South could cross to the ♠K and discard his club losers on dummy's hearts as East follows. South could then cross to his hand in spades, draw the rest of East's trump, and run clubs.

Finally, if West discards on the first round of clubs South can either play to squeeze West in the red suits or, more simply, cash another top club and ruff a club in the dummy. South can then draw trump and later discard his remaining club loser on dummy's hearts (overtaking the ♥J).

notes: West leads the ♠9 against 6NT. After winning West's spade opening lead, South should lead high hearts from his hand in an attempt to drive out the ♥A and create a dummy entry to finesse in clubs. When West discards on the second round of hearts, it appears that this plan will not succeed.

East will also duck the third round of hearts and, if South tries to gain entry to the dummy by leading the ♦2 for a finesse, West will play the ♦Q to foil this plan. East has 3 clubs and dummy's single entry is not sufficient to finesse twice in that suit.

After East has ducked the first 3 rounds of hearts South must continue by cashing the ♠A. If West discards on this trick, East will be marked with 7 spades and 4 hearts. East will have only 2 clubs and a single finesse (and single dummy entry) will see South home.

If West follows to the second round of spades South leads the ♦2 and West must play the ♦Q to prevent a second entry to the dummy. South can succeed by allowing West to hold this trick! West cannot afford to return a club and his diamond return is won with dummy's ♦A. Dummy's remaining diamond winners are played.

Dummy's last diamond will squeeze East in 3 suits. A club discard will allow South to run the clubs with a single finesse. If instead East discards from either major, he will establish a winner in the dummy and the play of that card will squeeze East again.

This deal was taken from Adventures in Card Play by Géza Ottlik and Hugh Kelsey. If you enjoy the challenge of Level 5 Bridge Master deals you will certainly enjoy this book. In our opinion Adventures in Card Play is by far the best book ever written on (very) advanced card play technique.

notes: West leads the ♥6 against 6♠. West's heart opening lead, an obvious singleton based on East's 2♥ opening, is won in dummy. 2 rounds of trump reveal the 4-1 break. South should plan to lead hearts toward dummy at some point giving West a chance to ruff South's heart loser with his natural trump trick.

South will also have to discard his 2 club losers on dummy's diamonds. East's discard on the third round of diamonds gives South a complete count on the hand (West was dealt 4153 and East 1624). The fact that West was dealt 3 clubs will cause South to fail if he continues diamonds at this point.

The best South can do is to cross to the ♣A and lead a heart toward dummy. West will gratefully discard a club, allowing the dummy to win the trick. A club is ruffed in the closed hand and South crosses to the dummy in spades. When South tries to ruff dummy's last club West will be able to overruff and the contract will fail.

Once South finds out that West was dealt exactly 3 clubs, his only chance is to hope that both the ♣K and the ♣Q are with East and that West was dealt the ♣9. South should not cash the fourth round of diamonds. Instead, he should lead the ♣J or ♣10, forcing East to cover. South must then cross to the dummy in spades and cash dummy's remaining diamond for a club discard.

Dummy's remaining club honor is played. East must cover and South ruffs. South leads a heart toward the dummy and West is squeezed in an unusual way. If West ruffs that will be the only trick for the defense. If West discards his diamond, dummy will win the trick and South will be able to ruff dummy's last club for his 12th trick. Finally, if West discards his ♣9 dummy will win and the ♣8 can be used to discard South's heart loser.
This beautiful deal was composed by Pietro Bernasconi for the 1998 World Par Contest in Lille, France (which was won by Michael Rosenberg).

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 6NT. Assuming South can win 4 club tricks and that East has the ♦K, there still will be only 11 winners. An extra major suit trick will be required. Given West's Michaels cuebid South will not be able to establish an extra trick in a major.

Some kind of squeeze against West will be required, but the entry situation is not appropriate for any common 2-loser squeezes. If South ducks a spade trick to West at some point in an attempt to rectify the count for a simple squeeze, West will play another heart to destroy the entry required for such an ending.

South's only chance is to play for an entry shifting squeeze (which gets its name from what will transpire in the club suit). South will lead the ♣K in the above position squeezing West in the majors. If West discards a spade the ♣9 is unblocked from dummy to create an extra entry to the South hand. A spade is played to the ♠K and South returns to the closed hand in clubs in order to surrender a spade trick to West. South's ♥K and winning spade will take the last 2 tricks.

If West chooses to discard a heart (instead of a spade) on the ♣K, South must play dummy's small club on this trick, preserving the ♣9 as a dummy entry. South unblocks the ♥K and crosses to the dummy in clubs (or spades) in order to surrender a heart trick to West. Dummy's remaining hearts are winners and the ♠K remains as a dummy entry.

The entry mechanism required for this squeeze to operate is extremely delicate. There is only 1 layout of the East-West clubs in which South can reach a position equivalent to the above and South must play his cards in a precise order.

South must start by winning West's heart opening lead with the ♥A. South must then take 2 diamond finesses, carefully unblocking the suit so that the lead remains in the dummy. If East covers the second round of diamonds with the ♦K, South must cross to the dummy in diamonds.

West must have a doubleton ♣10 (or doubleton ♣Q10) in order for South to reach the desired ending. The ♣J should be led from dummy and passed if East follows small. South continues with a club to his hand, unblocking the ♣9 or ♣8 from dummy. South has reached the desired ending. The ♣K will squeeze West with dummy playing either the ♣9 or the ♣5 depending on West's choice of discards.

Note that the contract cannot be made if West was dealt a doubleton ♣Q. The best South can do is cash the ♣A and ♣K, unblocking the ♣8 and ♣9 from dummy. South continues clubs, but West can defeat the contract by discarding a heart. There is no entry flexibility in this ending as dummy's ♣J must win the trick. South now lacks the entries required to unblock, establish, and cash the heart suit.

If South had tried unblocking hearts before playing the third round of clubs, West could defeat the contract by discarding a spade. The bottom line is South cannot succeed if West has a doubleton ♣Q. South must play West for a doubleton ♣10 in order for the entry shifting squeeze to be possible.

notes: West leads the ♦10 against 4♥. East wins the ♦A and switches to a trump. South will need West to have the ♠K for the contract to have a chance. That leaves East with the ♣AKQ (and ♦AQ) for his 1NT opening. If East has 3 trumps he will be able to prevent South from ruffing a club in the dummy.

In order for South to counter this threat, South must win East's heart shift in the closed hand and unblock the ♦K. South continues by finessing in spades and ruffing a diamond in the closed hand. East is marked with the outstanding ♦Q and South can make his contract with an unusual 3-suit squeeze.

South must play a spade to dummy's ♠A and ruff a spade (East pitches a club) before losing a club trick to East. East must return a trump which South wins in dummy as West's discard confirms the 3-1 trump break. When dummy's last spade is led East is squeezed in 3 suits.

If East ruffs, South can overruff and later ruff a club in dummy. If instead East discards the ♦Q, South can ruff high and draw trump with dummy's ♥Q to enjoy the dummy's newly established diamond winner. Finally, if East discards a club on dummy's last spade, South ruffs low and surrenders a club trick to East. South will win the last 2 tricks regardless of which suit East returns.

If East had followed with the ♦Q and West had followed small when South ruffed the third round of diamonds, West would be marked with the ♦9 (from his lead of the ♦10). In this case South must concede a club trick at once, win East's necessary trump return, and play a second round of clubs to East. East must return a trump, but South can win in hand and cash the remaining hearts. The play of South's last heart will squeeze West in spades and diamonds.
